paper_metadata.title: Decreasing Zr content to improve tensile properties of non-equiatomic TiZrHfNb medium entropy alloys with transformation-induced plasticity

evidence.quote: Here, reducing Zr content in Ti(80-x)ZrxHf10Nb10 (at.%) alloys was demonstrated to destabilize the BCC phase and trigger the BCC to hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase transformation.

Alloy ingots with three different compositions Ti(80-x)ZrxHf10Nb10 (x = 40, 30 and 20, in at.%) were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (better than 99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. At least five times remelting was used to ensure chemical homogeneity of the buttons.
The arc-melted alloys were homogenized at 1100 ◦C for 2h followed by water-quenching.
The homogenized alloys were cut into plates with a thickness of 8 mm, then cold rolled to sheets with a total thickness reduction of 80%.

To acquire a fine equiaxed microstructure, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at 900 ◦C for 30 min followed by water-quenching. All the heat treatments were conducted in a tube furnace with high-purity argon flowing to inhibit the oxidation of the samples.

For Zr30 alloy, the modest but steady straining hardening postpones the onset of necking until 35% uniform tensile strain.
For Zr20 alloy, the activation of residual BCC (based on the EBSD/TEM results in Fig. 4) to HCP phase transformation is considered to induce the first yielding around 380 MPa during the tensile test.
For Zr30 alloy, the BCC → HCP transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect contributes to the steady work hardening and high tensile strain.

According to the dynamic Hall-Petch theory, the transformed HCP bands refine the initial BCC grains along with increasing the density of phase interface, which effectively reduces the mean free path of dislocations and limits dislocation glide
In brief, the deformation of Zr40 alloy is mainly controlled by dislocation glide, resulting in high yield strength and poor strain hardening ability.
